transitory

/TRAN-suh-tor-ee/ — rhymes with 'memory' but slower · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Transitory describes something that lasts only a short time before passing away.

Fame from a viral video is usually transitory, gone within a month.

Example

The snow from the winter storm fell thick and white across the fields, but the March sun melted it all away within a week—a transitory blanket of cold.

Transitory captures more than just 'temporary'—it emphasizes the inevitability of fading. The snow didn't just disappear; it naturally and gradually passed away. Saying 'temporary snow' would miss that sense of natural, irreversible decline.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fleeting: Fleeting describes what passes so quickly it barely registers — a fleeting glance, a fleeting smile, gone in seconds. Transitory allows more time: a transitory fad can hold on for weeks. What transitory stresses is not speed but certainty — the fading is built into the thing's nature.

short-lived: Short-lived is the plain measurement word: it says only that something did not last long, with no hint of why. Transitory says more — the thing was always going to pass, because fading is part of its nature, the way a sandcastle is doomed by the tide.

passing: Passing describes something already moving through and on its way out — a passing shower, a passing mood — and it is the gentlest of these words. Transitory makes a stronger claim about the thing itself: lasting only a short time is part of what it is.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

permanent: lasting forever, never expected to change

enduring: continuing strong through long stretches of time

Where it sits · how much fading is built in

momentary → temporary → transitory → ephemeral

momentary vs. transitory: Momentary is the quickest of these words — gone in a second — while transitory describes something that lingers a little longer but is still destined to pass.

temporary vs. transitory: Temporary is weaker in feeling than transitory: temporary simply says something will end, while transitory stresses that fading away is part of its very nature.

ephemeral vs. transitory: Ephemeral goes even further than transitory; a transitory fad may last a few weeks, but something ephemeral, like a mayfly's life, vanishes within a single day.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — trans-: across, beyond (Latin)

Root — it: to go (from ire) (Latin)

Suffix — -ory: having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Trans- means 'across,' the Latin root it- means 'to go' (from ire), and -ory means 'having the quality of' — so transitory literally describes something 'having the quality of going across': it passes through and moves on rather than staying.

Use the root in a new word: transit: The tracking page showed the package still in transit, three days out from the warehouse and two from her door.

Word Choice

neutral

Transitory fits when something is clearly fading or will naturally disappear—interest, moods, trends, effects. For something brief but deliberately kept short (like a temporary visit or job), 'temporary' is clearer. For something impossibly delicate and poetic, reach for 'ephemeral' instead.
